title: Benchmark launches defence battery demand forecast
gist: Benchmark's first defence battery demand dataset sizes 2025 global military battery demand at 4.34GWh, with drones already ~40% of it after climbing from ~15% in 2020 — a small but strategically loaded slice where procurement-security rules push supply chains toward domestication and where low-volume, highly specialised cell makers can win rather than lose.

insights.claim: Global battery demand from defence applications totalled 4.34GWh in 2025, a volume that remains a small fraction of the overall battery industry.
insights.speaker: Benchmark Team
insights.so_what: Anchors the addressable size of the 'defence battery' narrative — at ~4GWh it is a margin and strategic-optionality story, not a volume story, so treat pure-play defence battery valuations accordingly.
insights.quote: In 2025, battery demand from defence applications totalled 4.34GWh globally.
insights.locator: How large is defence battery demand?

insights.claim: Drones generated just under 40% of 2025 defence battery demand, up from roughly 15% in 2020, making them the dominant single driver of the segment.
insights.speaker: Benchmark Team
insights.so_what: The mix shift is the signal: drone cell formats and chemistries — not vehicle or base storage specs — now set the direction of defence cell demand growth.
insights.quote: Just shy of 40% of this demand was generated by drones, a share that’s rapidly climbed from around 15% in 2020
insights.locator: How large is defence battery demand?

insights.claim: Defence battery demand is broadening beyond drones into on-base power generation redundancy, next generation fighter jets, submarines and ground vehicles, while military personnel power demand stays comparatively steady.
insights.speaker: Benchmark Team
insights.so_what: Gives a segment map for screening suppliers — the growth is in drones and base storage, while soldier power is the stable annuity-like slice.
insights.locator: Alongside rapidly growing drone and unmanned

themes.theme: Ukraine as the drone-warfare regime change

insights.claim: Russia's 2022 invasion of Ukraine reset the parameters of drone warfare and pushed the industry to an output of tens of thousands of drones per day.
insights.speaker: Benchmark Team
insights.so_what: Daily-consumption drone warfare converts batteries from a durable-good input into a consumable munition input — a fundamentally different, restocking-driven demand curve.
insights.quote: Russia’s invasion of Ukraine in 2022 set new parameters in drone warfare and has led to an industry outputting tens of thousands of drones daily.

insights.claim: The supply chains behind this new class of drone weaponry were built at speed and must evolve constantly, implying low incumbency protection and repeated qualification cycles for cell suppliers.
insights.speaker: Benchmark Team
insights.so_what: Fast-iterating specs favour agile cell makers over scale incumbents; watch for supplier churn rather than assuming locked-in multi-year contracts.
insights.quote: Supply chains around this new class of weapons have had to build quickly and evolve constantly.
insights.locator: Supply chains around this new class

insights.claim: Major military powers globally are moving from observing drone warfare to preparing scaled-up domestic drone manufacturing capability.
insights.speaker: Benchmark Team
insights.so_what: Signals a coming wave of nationally-funded drone plants — the derived demand lands on domestic cell, cathode and anode capacity, not on the cheapest global supplier.

insights.claim: Soldier power and base energy storage are large defence demand drivers precisely because their technical requirements align with batteries already available from larger commercial markets.
insights.speaker: Benchmark Team
insights.so_what: These segments are addressable by existing commercial cell lines with little retooling — the cheapest path for a battery maker to book defence revenue.
insights.locator: Beyond drones, soldier power and energy storage

insights.claim: Reliance on commercial-market batteries is a double-edged sword for defence buyers because procurement security risks force greater domestication of supply chains.
insights.speaker: Benchmark Team
insights.so_what: Expect defence demand to be priced above commercial equivalents for the same cell, with the premium accruing to domestically-qualified suppliers rather than lowest-cost Asian output.
insights.quote: However, this can be a double-edged sword as procurement security risks dictate greater domestication of supply chains.
insights.locator: However, this can be a double-edged sword

insights.claim: In defence batteries, low production volume can be an advantage rather than a weakness, opening the market to niche manufacturers that cannot compete on gigafactory scale.
insights.speaker: Benchmark Team
insights.so_what: Inverts the usual battery-industry scale thesis — screen small specialist cell makers for defence exposure instead of assuming only the largest players capture it.
insights.quote: where low volumes can be an advantage not a weakness
insights.locator: More niche manufacturers are now realising

insights.claim: Highly specialised battery systems designed for narrow parameter sets in weapons and vehicles will not be available off the shelf yet remain critical to militaries, creating defensible bespoke niches.
insights.speaker: Benchmark Team
insights.so_what: Bespoke, spec-locked programmes carry higher margin and stickier design-wins than commodity cell supply — the better place to hunt for defence battery pricing power.

insights.claim: Benchmark's defence modelling combines active conflict tracking with procurement and development programmes for next generation weaponry, spanning consumable FPV-style interceptor and attack drones plus larger unmanned aerial, underwater and surface systems.
insights.speaker: Benchmark Team
insights.so_what: Conflict-tracking as a live model input means the forecast is event-sensitive — revisions will follow escalation or ceasefire news, not just annual procurement budgets.
insights.quote: Benchmark’s detailed defence modelling incorporates active conflict tracking alongside procurement and development programmes of next generation weaponry.

insights.claim: Defence application coverage is delivered inside Benchmark's Non-road Mobile Machinery datafile with forecast GWh and chemistry share running out to 2050, with company and manufacturer profiling deferred to the 2026 NRMM report later this year.
insights.speaker: Benchmark Team
insights.so_what: Chemistry-share forecasts to 2050 are the tradable part — they show whether defence pulls toward LFP, high-nickel or specialist chemistries; named-company exposure only arrives with the later 2026 edition.
